title: Scaled throttle explainer and customer action brief
body:
Purpose:
This doc is a concise, customer-oriented explanation of a recent scaled-throttle event that affected a subset of heavy-throughput customers. It contains: a short public-friendly status snippet for the status page, recommended actions customers can take immediately, a customer-facing postmortem summary suitable for email/reporting, and a short timeline + next steps we will take. Use these verbatim or adapt to account teams' tone.

Executive summary (one paragraph):
On 2029-03-17 at ~21:40 UTC we observed sustained request bursts from several integrations which triggered an automated scaled-throttling policy. Customers experienced elevated 429/503 errors and increased tail latency for requests sent during the burst window (~21:40–22:15 UTC). The runtime applied protective throttles to preserve cluster availability; this prevented broader outage but caused degraded experience for some tenants. No customer data was lost. We validated correctness of request routing and resumed normal service by 22:20 UTC after circuit-control adjustments and capacity smoothing.

What customers likely saw (bullet list):
- Short intermittent 429 responses and Retry-After headers for some requests.
- Occasional 503/timeout on streaming sessions (partial responses may have been truncated).
- Longer than typical completion times for requests that were allowed through (higher p95/p99).
- No change to inference outputs for accepted requests (no data corruption).

Why this happened (plain language):
- A cloud customer integration generated a high-frequency burst pattern (many concurrent requests per second with long token windows) that matched an emergent, previously-unseen tail workload pattern.
- Our scaled-throttle safety layer (intent: prevent noisy neighbor effects and avoid destabilizing GPU pools) reacted conservatively and reduced request concurrency for affected tenants.
- The safety layer worked as designed to prevent cascade failure, but it was too aggressive for this particular mix of workloads.

Immediate steps we took (what we did during the incident):
- Identified and isolated the burst sources via request traces and token-level diagnostics.
- Tuned per-tenant concurrency limits and temporarily increased burst capacity for specific dedicated pools.
- Adjusted scaled-throttle heuristics to relax on long-token-window requests while preserving cross-tenant safety.
- Applied temporary routing overrides to route affected traffic to unaffected GPU pools in a different region to lower queueing.

Customer actions we recommend (short, actionable):
- Implement exponential backoff on 429s using the Retry-After header when present; recommended base: 250ms, multiplier 2.0, max backoff 8s.
- Add idempotency tokens for request retries where possible to prevent duplicate side effects.
- Reduce synchronous burst concurrency: stagger client retry jitter and limit concurrent inflight requests per host to a conservative cap (example: 12 inflight requests per client instance).
- For long-running prompts, use streaming partials or prefix caching where supported to trim per-request token spikes.
- If you run extremely bursty throughput, consider reserving Dedicated capacity or enabling a dedicated model variant to avoid shared throttles.

Status page snippets (pick appropriate length):
- Early update (short): "Partial service interruption for text generation in US region due to protective throttling; engineers are mitigating and normal service is expected shortly."
- Follow-up (mid): "We observed high request bursts that triggered automatic protection measures for some customers, resulting in elevated 429 responses and increased latency between 21:40–22:15 UTC. We applied routing and throttle adjustments and are monitoring system stability."
- Resolution (short): "Incident mitigated at 22:20 UTC. Protective throttles relaxed and traffic normalized. No data loss; see full customer summary for recommended actions."

Customer-facing postmortem summary (template for account teams):
Title: Scaled-throttle protective measures — customer impact summary (2029-03-17)
Summary: At 21:40 UTC on 2029-03-17, automated protection logic reduced concurrency for a subset of tenants in the US GPU pool to maintain cluster health. Customers saw transient 429s/503s and higher latency during the burst window. We intervened manually and by adapting heuristics; normal service resumed at 22:20 UTC.
Root cause (concise): An unanticipated burst pattern from a high-throughput integration interacted with an overly conservative throttling heuristic for long-window token requests.
Scope: Affecting approximately 6 mid-to-high-volume tenants in the US region for ~35 minutes; small percentage of requests returned 429/503.
Impact: Elevated client-side error rates and increased latency; no request results were corrupted or lost, and all accepted responses were correct.
Remediation & next steps:
- Short-term: throttle heuristics relaxed and per-tenant overrides applied for affected pools.
- Mid-term (2–3 weeks): implement more nuanced heuristics that consider token-window length and client concurrency signals; add targeted anomaly detection to differentiate short bursts vs sustained floods.
- Structural (quarter): new self-service controls for tenants to declare expected burst profiles and opt into reserved throughput.

Timeline (high level):
- 21:38 UTC — pre-incident anomaly detection alert (minor).
- 21:40 UTC — automatic scaled-throttle triggered for multiple tenants.
- 21:45–22:05 UTC — engineers trace culprit integrations and apply temporary per-tenant overrides.
- 22:12 UTC — routing adjustments send select traffic to alternate pools.
- 22:20 UTC — system returns to nominal throughput and tail latency improves.

Monitoring & how we validated resolution: 
- Cleared repeat 429 spikes across tenants and observed p99 latency return to baseline for the affected pools.
- Replayed synthetic steady-state traffic and verified throttles did not re-trigger under similar token windows.

Q&A for account teams (common customer questions + suggested responses):
Q: Will we get credited for the degraded period?
A: For customers with Dedicated reservations we will assess SLA impact per contract; for Hosted customers we will evaluate case-by-case and offer goodwill credits where appropriate. Ask accounts to open a billing ticket referencing JIRA-REDS-4127.

Q: Could this happen again?
A: We have implemented immediate mitigations and a roadmap to reduce recurrence risk (see remediation). We expect recurrence probability to be low once mid-term heuristics are deployed, but we advise customers with bursty workloads to consider Dedicated capacity to eliminate shared safety policies.

Q: How can I get help if my integration is affected?
A: Contact your CS lead or open a support ticket with logs (request-ids if available), approximate time window, and whether you observed Retry-After headers. We can apply targeted overrides for critical tenants while longer-term fixes roll out.

Suggested action email subject lines (short):
- "Action recommended: adjust retry/backoff to avoid burst-triggered throttles"
- "Notice: transient throttling event — summary & next steps"

Appendix: Technical details for engineers (short bullets for customers who want more):
- Scaled-throttle considers per-tenant inflight request count, request token window, and observed queueing. Previously the heuristic weighted recent inflight count heavily; we added a token-window normalization factor to reduce false positives on long-window requests.
- Retry-After responses include a hint header X-RI-Suggested-Wait with a suggested backoff in ms for better client behavior.

Contact & escalation: 
- Primary CS contact: Ava Chen (ava@redwood.ai)
- On-call engineering lead: Diego Morales (pager: EM-ops)

Notes for internal use:
- Use the status snippets verbatim on status.redwood.ai and the account-facing template for high-value customers.
- Track follow-up for mid-term heuristic changes under JIRA-REDS-4199 and include CS owners in design reviews.

Document history: 2029-03-18 initial draft; 2029-03-20 updated with timeline and remediation commitments.
